81: Location decides a great deal of the plan's operating viability. We want a spot with real evening foot traffic, ideally on a block that already has bars and restaurants, so guests arrive by habit rather than by advertising. A second-generation space of roughly 2,400 square feet covers the dining room, the kitchen and a patio, and it keeps revenue per square foot healthy while the service flow stays efficient. The layout puts a prominent bar at the center of the room, long enough to serve as the main sales engine and as the spot for a quick drink and a plate, with tables around it for full service. The kitchen sits at the back with proper ventilation and a short, direct line to the bar, so small plates reach guests at the bar and on the patio without long waits.
82: The kitchen is deliberately short, and it should be sized for efficient small-plates production, not for a full restaurant menu. The core equipment is a gas griddle, a fryer with a filtration system and a combi or standard oven, all under a Type I hood with a fire suppression system and served by a grease interceptor, which is why the plumbing and hood line in the budget is significant. Behind the bar, the build includes underbar stations for speed, back-bar coolers for beer, mixers and garnish, and a draft beer system with enough lines for a rotating tap list. A draft installer, sometimes arranged through your distributor, installs the lines and the glycol cooling; budget it yourself and plan regular line cleaning. Furniture is a mix of tables, high-tops and bar stools, plus patio seating when the lease allows it.
83: Supplier choices should balance quality, price and reliability. In most states, alcohol moves through the three-tier system: producers sell to licensed distributors, distributors sell to licensed retailers like us, and we sell to guests. That means you buy beer, wine and spirits only from a licensed distributor, and you should compare delivery days, minimums and payment terms before committing to any single one. Tied-house rules also limit what a producer or distributor can give a bar for free, so do not build the plan on free taps or free equipment in exchange for exclusivity. For produce, bread and proteins, a local wholesale market or a broadline distributor gives the kitchen consistent quality. Keep at least two suppliers for each critical category so one late truck never shuts down a Friday night.
84: Service flow has to handle two different rhythms: the early happy hour crowd and the dinner-and-drinks rush that builds after it. At the bar, bartenders prep garnishes, juices and batched cocktails before opening, and the kitchen preps cold small plates ahead so a drink and a plate leave the pass within minutes. Hot plates are cooked to order against a clear ticket-time target. In the dining room, servers greet each table quickly, take the drink order first and suggest plates that match what guests are drinking. Handheld POS devices let servers and bartenders send orders straight to the kitchen and the bar, which keeps the floor moving. The plan models {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day across {{aforo}} seats, and the evening is where those turns are won or lost.
85: Inventory control starts at the bar. Count liquor, beer and wine at least weekly, compare actual usage with what your POS says was sold, and calculate pour cost by category. BevSpot reports that pour cost for a typical bar runs between 18% and 24%, with category medians of about 24% for beer, 15% for spirits and 28% for wine, so you can see which category is drifting. A big gap between theoretical and actual usage points to over-pouring, waste, comps that were never rung in or theft. The workbook models beverage cost at {{food_cost_bebida}}, so treat that number as a target you check every week. On the kitchen side, order daily in small quantities, use a daily special to move products that are close to their date, and keep a waste log. Stagger staffing so weekends and events get extra hands without raising fixed labor all week.
88: A neighborhood bar lives or dies by its team: the right people in the right roles, flexible hours and clear responsibilities. The US restaurant and bar industry is crowded with small independent operators, so versatility and role clarity make the difference between a profitable place and a chaotic one. The organization we propose is lean on purpose. It is built around what each shift needs and leaves room to adjust as we learn how guests actually use the room.
89: The roster in the workbook's "Staffing" tab has {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, spread across the critical functions of management, production and service. The owner and general manager is accountable for the whole business: scheduling, cost control, supplier relationships, hiring and daily supervision. This role is essential in a place where the value proposition includes a cocktail list, a thoughtful wine selection and a draft lineup that need real product knowledge and the ability to recommend. In the early months the owner will probably cover shifts, so plan on that and keep a relief cover role in the budget.
90: The kitchen is led by a kitchen lead who knows how to produce small plates quickly and consistently. Shareable plates reward speed, repeatable presentation and the ability to work under pressure during a rush, and these are skills that separate a strong line cook from a cook trained for a long restaurant menu. The kitchen lead builds the menu with the owner, writes the prep lists and controls food cost. The production team is completed by a line and prep cook, who prepares the cold plates and the mise en place for the evening and keeps quality steady across the dinner service.
91: The bar and floor need a specific setup for a venue with a prominent bar and an after-work crowd. The bartenders are the most strategic hires: they pour accurately, know the cocktail, draft and wine lists well enough to recommend, and can handle several orders at once while still talking with guests. Their consistency protects pour cost and their personality builds regulars. Servers cover the dining room and the patio, taking care of dinner guests and groups, while barbacks keep the bar stocked, glassware moving and ice, garnish and kegs ready, so the bartenders can stay behind the bar and sell. Weekend extra hands, when needed, come from the barback pool.
92: The prep cook supports production, cleans and portions raw ingredients, keeps the stations organized and helps with mise en place. Weekend and event coverage comes from the barback and weekend extra role, plus relief cover, which absorbs the Friday, Saturday and Sunday peaks without locking the plan into a heavy fixed payroll on the slower days of the week. Part-time and flexible shifts are common in the industry, and they let the schedule follow real demand.
93: Labor costs have three parts. First, wages: the federal minimum wage is {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for full-time work, and your state or city may set a higher floor, so check both. Second, employer payroll taxes, which the workbook models at {{cargas_pct}} of wages. Third, tips. The workbook does not use tip credit: bartenders, barbacks and servers are modeled on a base wage of at least $15 an hour, with tips treated as extra income for the team. Under federal rules, employers can pay $2.13 an hour and claim a tip credit of up to $5.12 where state law allows it, but California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska, Minnesota, Montana and Nevada do not allow tip credit at all, according to the US Department of Labor. Modeling a base wage keeps the plan conservative, and you can change it in the workbook if your state allows a tip credit.
94: Training is a real advantage in a market where guests notice consistency. The program should cover draft beer service and line cleaning, cocktail specs and pour control, small-plates timing and presentation, and food safety, with special attention to the nine major allergens, which the FDA Food Code, as adopted by your state, requires you to be able to identify and communicate to guests. Responsible alcohol service training such as TIPS or ServSafe Alcohol should be on the list for every bartender, server and manager. Finally, teach servers to suggest pairings and shareable plates, because a thoughtful recommendation lifts the check without any pressure on the guest.
95: Scheduling a bar means covering a happy hour, a dinner rush and a late evening, each with a different pace, so the schedule should follow the forecast rather than the calendar. Staggered shifts and a clear on-call or relief system let you add a bartender on a patio night and trim hours on a slow Tuesday. Retention matters in an industry with high turnover, so competitive wages, predictable schedules, a professional atmosphere and room to grow into lead roles pay for themselves in quality of service and in training costs you do not have to repeat. Check your state and local labor rules on scheduling, breaks and overtime before you publish the first schedule.
98: The total startup investment in the example case is {{inversion_total}}, made up of {{capex}} of startup costs and a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. Cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The plan is financed with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a loan of {{prestamo}} at a nominal rate of {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. The bigger lines are the second-generation build-out ({{inv_obra}}), the bar build ({{inv_barra}}), plumbing, grease interceptor and hood ({{inv_campana}}), electrical and HVAC ({{inv_instalaciones}}), refrigeration ({{inv_frio}}), the draft system ({{inv_grifos}}) and kitchen equipment ({{inv_cocina}}). The liquor license and local permits are budgeted at {{inv_licencia}} as a non-quota state example, and opening inventory at {{inv_stock}}. Restaurant365 puts the cost of opening a bar at $100,000 to $850,000 or more, so your real number will depend on your state, your lease and your build-out. Lenders may offer an SBA 7(a) loan or a conventional bank loan, but no lender can promise approval.
99: Year-1 revenue is projected at {{ventas_a1}} excluding sales tax, from {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at an average check of {{ticket}} over {{dias}} days a year. Year 2 grows volume by {{crecimiento_a2}} to {{clientes_a2}} covers a day and {{ventas_a2}} in revenue, as regulars build and the patio season settles in. Year 3 adds another {{crecimiento_a3}}, reaching {{clientes_a3}} covers a day and {{ventas_a3}}. The sales mix is {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverages, and alcohol accounts for {{alcohol_pct}} of beverage sales. Because beverages carry the lower cost, this mix is what gives the model its margin. If your concept leans more toward food, change the mix in the "0. Assumptions" tab and watch the margin move.
100: The cost structure is a bar's, not a restaurant's. Food cost is modeled at {{food_cost_comida}} of food sales and beverage cost at {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales, which gives cost of goods of {{cogs_pct}} of total sales; with card fees, disposables and contingency the variable costs reach {{costes_variables_pct}}, for a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales and occupancy is {{ocupacion_pct}}. Prime cost, meaning cost of goods plus labor, comes out at {{prime_cost_pct}} in year 1. That is below the 60% to 65% that Restaurant365 cites for full-service restaurants, and the reason is simple: a bar sells mostly drinks, and drinks cost far less to make than a plate of food. Tips are not in this number, since the base wages already cover the team, and employer FICA on reported tips is not modeled either (largely offset by the FICA tip credit; ask your CPA). Card fees, disposables and contingency are variable costs counted before the gross margin, so the workbook gives you the whole picture. If your pour cost drifts upward, prime cost is the first number that moves, which is why we track it weekly.
101: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, equal to {{equilibrio_ventas}} of annual revenue. The number that matters most for survival is cash break-even, where loan payments are counted and depreciation is not: {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year. The projected volume sits {{holgura_caja_pct}} above that level. The loan carries a payment of {{cuota_anual}} a year, and the DSCR, the ratio of cash available for debt service to the debt payments due, is {{dscr_a1}} in year 1 and never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the loan term. The workbook sets its limit at {{dscr_limite}}, and lenders typically look for about {{dscr_objetivo}} or higher. If your own DSCR lands under that mark, lower the loan, raise the equity or recheck your volume before you talk to a bank. The lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, reached in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}.
102: The "Scenarios" tab tests three situations. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days, for revenue of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax loss of {{pesimista_perdida}}. Operations lose money even before depreciation and interest (about {{pesimista_perdida_operativa}}), so the loan payment comes out of the working capital reserve: the bar ends year 1 with an estimated {{pesimista_caja}} of cash, and a second year like that would run out of cash. The base case is the one described above. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_clientes}} covers a day at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days, with revenue of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. In the base case the project returns its investment before debt in a payback of {{payback}}. Read the pessimistic case as a stress test: if it is plausible in your market, you need a bigger reserve, a smaller loan or a smaller opening.
103: The financial viability of the project depends on three factors. The first is location, because covers drive everything and a bar on a quiet block will not reach break-even. The second is pour cost and waste control, because a few points of drift in beverage cost cost far more than any single expense line. The third is a differentiated offer that justifies the check, from the cocktail list and the room to the service. With disciplined management, the analysis shows a path to profitability within the three-year horizon of the workbook, but nothing in it is a guarantee: you should replace our example numbers with your own quotes, your own lease and your own local costs, and let the Excel workbook recalculate.
106: Opening a bar in the United States means working through several layers of government, and the order matters. You form your entity, usually an LLC, with your state's Secretary of State, and at the federal level you get an Employer Identification Number from the IRS at no cost. Also at the state level you register for a seller's permit or sales tax account, and your alcohol license comes from a state agency. At the county and city level you need a business license, zoning approval and building permits for the build-out. Check zoning before you sign a lease, because the wrong zone can block a bar entirely. After the build-out, the city issues a certificate of occupancy, which you need before you open the doors.
107: The liquor license is the critical path. It is issued by a state agency, often called the ABC or the liquor control board, and it usually needs local approval as well. Classes vary by state, but the main choice is between a beer and wine license, which starts at about $3,000, and a full liquor license, which Poster puts at $12,000 to $400,000. In states with a quota, you generally buy or transfer an existing license at market price, and that can be an order of magnitude more: R Street reports that bar licenses in Boston sell for north of $450,000. The workbook budgets {{inv_licencia}} for a state without a quota as an example only, so replace it with your state's real fees. Start right after signing the lease, because it often takes 3 to 12 months. A license bought from another owner is generally an intangible asset, so ask your CPA how to treat it.
108: The health department comes next. Most jurisdictions require a plan review before you build the kitchen, then a food establishment permit and an inspection before you open. You will need a Certified Food Protection Manager on staff, and food handler cards for the rest of the team where your state or county requires them. Most states follow a version of the FDA Food Code, and food law requires you to be able to identify the nine major allergens. In the kitchen, cooking with grease requires a Type I hood with a fire suppression system listed to UL 300 and installed under NFPA 96, a grease interceptor sized by the plumbing code and a fire marshal inspection. Post the required public notices, including the health permit, the liquor license and the labor law posters, where guests and staff can see them.
109: Liability is the part of owning a bar that surprises new owners. Under dram shop laws, a bar can be held responsible for harm caused by a guest who was served while visibly intoxicated or underage, and liquor liability insurance exists to cover that risk. Insureon reports a median of $2,039 a year for small bars, though a bar of this size will pay more, so the workbook budgets {{seguros_anual}} a year for general liability, liquor liability and property together. Responsible service training such as TIPS or ServSafe Alcohol, along with ID-checking procedures, is required by many states and insurers and is the best protection you can build into daily operations. If you plan a sidewalk café or patio, ask the city whether it needs its own permit, since outdoor seating is often regulated separately from the interior.
110: Playing music in a bar requires public performance licenses, which in the United States means working with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC for recorded or live music. Live bands or a DJ may also require a local entertainment permit, and a noise ordinance will limit how loud the patio and the room can be. Closing time and last call are set by your state and often by your city, so your actual hours, and the staffing hours in the workbook, depend on local law. Finally, post the labor law notices and keep your employment paperwork in order. If you are planning to open in the United Kingdom, the framework is different: you would need a premises licence and a personal licence under the Licensing Act 2003, you register the food business with the local council 28 days before opening and receive a Food Hygiene Rating (FHIS in Scotland), VAT at 20% applies to your sales, and you must be able to declare the 14 allergens.
113: The market opportunity rests on three pillars that do not depend on fashion. First, a neighborhood bar with a short kitchen creates a repeatable habit: a modest check that invites frequent visits, which is the real engine of a bar's revenue. Second, guests want an easy local place with real drinks and real food, and happy hour has become a daily ritual for after-work crowds. Third, the format scales smartly: the bar sells the margin and the small plates keep guests longer. A neighborhood bar with small plates takes that traditional format and makes the experience more thoughtful, without losing the approachable spirit that makes the volume possible.
114: The risks are manageable but need active attention. Location is the biggest one, and the neighborhood you choose will drive results more than any other decision, so favor blocks with steady foot traffic near offices, residential density or entertainment. Competition in the bar category is real, which calls for a clear difference in product, atmosphere or service. The liquor license is a timing risk: if it takes longer than planned, you are paying rent on a closed bar, so start it early, negotiate a license contingency in the lease and, if you expect it to take longer than the {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of pre-opening rent the workbook budgets, raise that number on "0. Assumptions". Over-pouring and waste can quietly erode margin, and seasonality matters on the patio and in tourist or college markets. We do not cite a national failure rate for bars, because we did not find a reliable source, but plan as if the first year will test every assumption.
115: The operating strengths of the model are significant. Beverages carry a lower cost than food, which is why prime cost lands at {{prime_cost_pct}} instead of the 60% to 65% typical of a full-service restaurant. The bar format serves many guests with a small team, seat turns of {{rotaciones_dia}} a day are achievable when the evenings are busy, and the patio adds capacity in good weather. The startup investment of {{capex}} in the example case sits within what the RestaurantOwner.com survey reports for a leased space, $110,000 to $550,000, as reported by Poster, which makes a reasonable debt structure possible when the DSCR clears the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders look for.
116: The roadmap is realistic if you keep to the order of the checklist. In the first months, form the LLC, get the EIN, search for the location and negotiate the lease. Right after signing, start the liquor license application, since it is the longest item and may take 3 to 12 months, and apply for building permits and health department plan review in parallel. The next phase is the build-out and equipment, the stage where cost overruns hide in every hospitality project, so keep the contingency. After that, hire and train the team, including responsible alcohol service training, and set up the POS, the inventory counts and your supplier accounts. Plan at least four weeks of pre-opening for menu tests, process adjustments and launch marketing before the doors open; pre-opening payroll and training come out of the working capital reserve.
117: Key indicators should include daily sales, covers per day, average check, seat turns, pour cost by category, labor as a percentage of sales, prime cost, repeat-guest rate and your online review score. Review them every month against the workbook and set progressive goals: reach cash break-even in the first months, consolidate a base of regulars over the first year and, in the second year, decide whether to improve profitability or consider expansion. Update the "0. Assumptions" tab with real numbers each quarter so the plan keeps working as a management tool, and not only as a document for a lender.
118: The three-year vision positions the bar as a local landmark, with loyal regulars, enough cash generation to reinvest in improvements and the potential to repeat the model if the results justify it. Year-3 revenue in the example is {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit is {{resultado_neto_a3}} (after the 25% C corporation tax example; pass-through owners set it to 0 and pay tax personally). These are projections from an example case, not promises, and your own numbers will differ. Use the workbook to test your concept, bring the plan to your lender and your partners, and update it as the real figures come in.
